list.listitem: Common causes of leg edema include heart failure, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), lymphedema, obesity, pregnancy, venous insufficiency, and medications (calcium channel blockers, NSAIDs, and corticosteroids). C
Begin by evaluating whether edema is unilateral or bilateral, painful or nonpainful, and acute or chronic. B
Routine evaluation of patients with chronic, bilateral leg edema includes CBC, UA, electrolytes, creatinine, blood sugar, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), and albumin. C
When DVT is suspected (acute, unilateral, typically painful) use the Wells clinical rule, D-dimer, and selective use of imaging to help confirm the diagnosis. A
Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) may be helpful for distinguishing heart failure from other causes of leg edema (but may vary from day to day). B

background.definition: Edema is a palpable swelling caused by an increase in intersitial fluid volume. There is underlying abnormal accumulation in connective tissues or serous cavities. It results from an imbalance in the Starling forces that balance hydrostatic pressures with tissue oncotic pressure, favoring extravasation of fluid into the interstitial space. It may result from a benign cause or a life-threatening illness. Lymphedema is characterized by an excessive accumulation of protein-rich fluid in the tissues.

list.listitem: Unilateral, acute: DVT, ruptured Baker's cyst, compartment syndrome.
Unilateral, chronic: venous insufficiency, lymphedema, pelvic tumor, and reflex sympathetic dystrophy.
Bilateral, acute: allergic reaction, trauma, burns, bilateral DVT, acute worsening of renal failure or heart failure.

Bilateral, chronic: venous insufficiency, pulmonary hypertension, heart failure, lymphedema, medications, premenstrual, pregnancy, edema, renal disease, idiopathic, dependent edema, anemia, or pre-eclampsia.

Edema occurs when there is an increase in capillary hydraulic pressure or capillary permeability, an increase in interstitial oncotic pressure, or a decrease in plasma oncotic pressure or a combination of all forces.
The kidneys play a central role in regulating sodium and water excretion to maintain body fluid homeostasis, so failure may result in edema.

Differential.Differential_Features: Bilateral edema, chronic: look for use of NSAIDs, calcium channel blockers, or hormones
Bilateral or unilateral edema: usually acute and painful

list.listitem: Key elements of the history are the duration of edema (acute or chronic), whether or not it is painful, and whether it is unilateral or bilateral. Associated breathlessness raises the concern for heart failure.
Suspect DVT if edema is unilateral or acute, if recent immobility or travel has occurred, if there is an active diagnosis of malignancy, or if recent trauma has occurred.
Suspect pulmonary hypertension leading to sleep apnea based on history of daytime somnolence, thick neck, and snoring.
Venous insufficiency typically improves overnight; lymphedema does not.
Take medication history (NSAIDs, calcium channel blockers, prednisone, hydralazine, estrogen, rosiglitazone and pioglitazone, monoamine oxidase [MAO] inhibitors).

Physical examination should evaluate for signs of infection or trauma. Tenderness to touch suggests cellulitis or DVT. Suspect heart failure if bilateral, chronic edema exists; the presence of S3 or jugular venous distension increases the likelihood significantly.
The Kaposi-Stemmer sign is an inability to tent the skin over the dorsum of the foot at the base of the second toe and suggests lymphedema.
Consider occult obstructive sleep apnea as a contributing factor to edema from right heart failure.
Unilateral edema (<72 hours): if DVT is suspected, use a combination of the, Wells rule D-dimer and an imaging study. See chapter on DVT for more detailed discussion.

Routine evaluation for patients with chronic, bilateral leg edema includes CBC, UA, electrolytes, creatinine, blood sugar, TSH, and albumin. These tests will identify causes such as anemia, renal disease (nephrotic syndrome), hypothyroidism, hypoalbuminia, and liver disease.
If heart failure is suspected or patient is older than 45 years: obtain, BNP, ECG, CXR, and echocardiogram. A normal BNP may not fully exclude the diagnosis of heart failure in some patients.
If liver disease is suspected: obtain hepatic transaminases and liver function tests (INR and plasma albumin).
If malignancy is suspected: obtain abdominal or pelvic CT.
If lymphedema is suspected: consider abdominal or pelvic CT.
Begin by assessing whether edema is acute or chronic, painful or nonpainful, and unilateral or bilateral. Unilateral edema, especially if painful, should be worked up for DVT.

The history and physical are directed toward the most common causes of edema: venous insufficiency, CHF, cirrhosis, kidney disease, pregnancy, and drug-induced edema. (See for a recommended approach to the differentiation of leg edema.)
Compression stocking therapy has been associated with reducing risk of cellulitis in patients with chronic venous insufficiency and edema (NNT=4).
